extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and beginning graduate students learning scheme-theoretic algebraic geometry (readers of Evan Chen's Napkin notes)
extracted.subtask_description: Worked examples and foundational statements about affine schemes, their points, stalks, residue fields, and morphisms of (locally) ringed spaces; includes exercises and many concrete Spec A computations to build intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nilpotents are the only issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Two functions f and g have the same value on all points of Spec A if and only if f − g is nilpotent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, when A is reduced (nilradical = (0)), the values f(p) as p ranges over Spec A determine f ∈ A. The prototype failure is exemplified by Spec C[x]/(x^2) where nonzero multiples of x vanish at the single point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nilradical and reduced ring
rubrics_metrics.description: The radical of the zero ideal p(0) is called the nilradical of A; elements of it are nilpotents. A is reduced if 0 is the only nilpotent, i.e. p(0) = (0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to decide when value-at-points determines global functions; examples: Spec C[x]/(x^2) (not reduced) versus reduced rings where values suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections determined by germs
rubrics_metrics.description: In any ringed space, a section is determined by its germs: on Spec A a function f ∈ A is determined by its germ in each stalk A_p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stronger than being determined by values in residue fields; the stalk contains more information (e.g., nilpotents) than the residue field, so knowing all germs determines a section even when knowing values at residue fields does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global sections of an affine scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: For X = Spec A, the global sections satisfy O_X(X) = A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact is used repeatedly (for instance to derive the Chinese remainder theorem from sheaf axioms) and underlies many computations of sections on distinguished opens and decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Points of Spec A correspond to prime ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of Spec A are prime ideals. Closed points often correspond to maximal ideals (e.g., (x−a) in k[x]); there is usually a generic point (0) when A is an integral domain; non-closed points correspond to non-maximal primes (e.g., primes defining irreducible subvarieties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this identification to draw and reason about the topology and types of points (closed, non-closed, generic) — examples include Spec k[x], Spec k[x,y], Spec Z, Spec R[x], and quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue fields and stalks
rubrics_metrics.description: The residue field at a point p is κ(p) ≅ A/p; the stalk at p is O_X,p ≅ A_p (localization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stalks generally carry strictly more information than residue fields (e.g., double point Spec k[x]/(x^2) has same residue field as the single point but a larger stalk). Use stalks to study local behavior (germs, allowed denominators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing closed sets, distinguished opens, and localizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Spec A/I is homeomorphic to the closed subset V(I) of Spec A; Spec A[1/f] corresponds to the distinguished open D(f); Spec A_p corresponds to the localization picture OSpec A,p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identifications let you translate algebraic operations (quotients, localizations, inverting elements) into topological/subspace operations on schemes; Exercise 86.12.1 and related sections illustrate these checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicompactness of Spec A
rubrics_metrics.description: Spec A is quasicompact for any ring A (Problem 85A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This topological property is a standard fact used in many arguments about coverings and descent on affine schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of local rings (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring R is a local ring iff for any x ∈ R, either x or 1 − x is a unit (Problem 85C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this algebraic test to recognize when a ring is local (e.g., localizations at primes). Problem 85D asks to describe R_m for a local ring R with maximal ideal m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms of ringed spaces (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism of ringed spaces (X,O_X) → (Y,O_Y) is a pair (π,π^#) where π : X → Y is continuous and for every open U ⊆ Y there is a ring homomorphism π^#_U : O_Y(U) → O_X(π^{-1}(U)) compatible with restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of π^# as the analogue of pullback of functions; in the concrete function-valued sheaf case π^# is composition (ϕ ↦ ϕ ◦ π). Compatibility with restriction diagrams is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced stalk morphisms and uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Given π : X → Y and p ∈ X with q = π(p), there is an induced map on stalks π^#_p : O_{Y,q} → O_{X,p}. Moreover π^# is uniquely determined by these stalk maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice one specifies stalk maps (which are fewer) and checks compatibility; not every choice of stalk morphisms produces a global π^#_U — a continuity/compatibility condition for sequences of compatible germs is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms of locally ringed spaces (local condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism of locally ringed spaces requires that for π(p)=q the induced map on stalks yields a field homomorphism π^#_p : κ(q) → κ(p) (equivalently (π^#_p)(m_{Y,q}) ⊆ m_{X,p}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric meaning: a germ vanishes at q iff its pullback vanishes at p; this preserves the notion of 'value at a point'. Exercise 87.3.2 discusses equivalence with local ring homomorphism condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism criterion for ringed spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A map of ringed spaces (π,π^#) is an isomorphism iff π is a homeomorphism and each induced stalk map π^#_p is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion lets you check isomorphisms locally on stalks together with the topological condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints on existence of morphisms (constant map examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete existence conditions: e.g., a constant morphism X = Spec R[x] → Spec R[y] sending all points to m = (y−3) forces y to map to 3 ∈ R[x]; in general, elements that are invertible as sections on some opens must map to invertible elements in the target ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stalk/global-section reasoning: if U excludes the image of a point then the preimage is empty and sections must map to zero ring; units on subopens force images to be units. Example 87.4.5 shows a constant map to (y^2+1) may not exist because units have nowhere to go.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization commutes with limits (principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Localization commutes with limits; used to justify decompositions and to compute stalks of limits (e.g., to decompose a stalk as fibered product of localizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in §86.14 to explain decomposition of k[x,y]/(xy) into a fibered product k[x] ×_k k[y] and to justify the analogous decomposition at stalks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf axioms give algebraic consequences (Chinese remainder example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheaf axioms and the identity O_X(X)=A yield algebraic decompositions: for X = Spec Z/60Z the sheaf computation gives Z/60Z ≅ Z/4Z × Z/3Z × Z/5Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret topological decomposition of Spec A into closed points as a product decomposition of global sections; this viewpoint provides geometric understanding/proofs of algebraic facts like the Chinese remainder theorem.
